title: Quote Templates & Document Generation

toc.text: Template anatomy: folders, sections, and blocks
The template layout: header, body, and footer
Hands-on walkthrough: build a quote template and generate a document

html:
A quote only becomes a sales tool when it is rendered as a clean, branded, customer-ready document. In the CPQ & Revenue Cloud Academy, quote templates bridge the gap between the structured pricing data held on a Quote and the polished PDF or Word file that actually ships to the buyer. This guide covers the template model, layout anatomy, tokens, multi-language output, document delivery, and e-signature — the "Quote Templates" domain that carries 7% of the Salesforce Certified CPQ Specialist exam blueprint.

In legacy CPQ the template objects live in the managed package namespace (SBQQ__QuoteTemplate__c, SBQQ__QuoteDocument__c, SBQQ__QuoteSection__c, SBQQ__QuoteBlock__c). Revenue Cloud / RLM re-expresses the same ideas on core objects, but the mental model — folders → templates → sections → blocks → rendered documents — is unchanged and is exactly what both certifications test.

Learning objectives

  • Explain where quote templates sit in the quote-to-cash lifecycle and why the presentation layer matters for win rate.
  • Distinguish standard and custom quote templates and know when to use each.
  • Describe template folders, sections, and blocks and how they compose into a page layout.
  • Build a header, body, and footer that pull live data from the Quote and QuoteLineItem records.
  • Use tokens, template variables, and formulas to substitute deal data into a document.
  • Design multi-language quote layouts and select the right language per account or locale.
  • Generate output documents (PDF and Word) and understand the document-generation lifecycle.
  • Configure e-signature so a signed quote flows back into the Quote and downstream records.

Why the document layer matters

The quote-to-cash chain ends where the buyer signs. Everything before it — configuration, pricing, discounts, approvals — produces numbers; the template produces meaning. A sales rep can configure a perfect bundle and still lose the deal if the PDF is cramped, outdated, or lists prices in the wrong currency. The quote document is simultaneously a legal offer, a commercial summary, and a marketing artifact.

From a process standpoint the document is also a control point. Quote approval may be gated on the generated document (nobody approves a quote they have not seen), and the final, agreed version of the document is what feeds Contract Generation. So the template layer connects the pricing engine to the contractual layer you will study in Contracts, Amendments & Renewals.

💡
Tip: Treat the quote template as part of your data model, not as a "print view". It consumes the same Quote and QuoteLineItem records the rest of your automation reads.

Template anatomy: folders, sections, and blocks

Each template in legacy CPQ is composed of three child collections. A template may contain many sections, and each section may contain many blocks, giving you a two-level grid much like a page layout.

Object (legacy)RoleExample
SBQQ__QuoteTemplateFolder__cGroups templates for admins"EMEA_Professional_Services"
SBQQ__QuoteTemplate__cThe top-level template, holds the default languageStandard hardware quote
SBQQ__QuoteSection__cA row in the layout; holds blocks side by side"Pricing Summary", "Terms"
SBQQ__QuoteBlock__cA cell in the grid; has a type and contentLine items table, custom text
SBQQ__QuoteDocument__cA generated, point-in-time copy of a quotePDF snapshot of quote Q-00123

The layout engine lays out blocks row by row. Within a section you arrange blocks left to right; the section wraps to the next row when the total block width exceeds the page width. Blocks can also repeat: a block bound to quote lines renders once per QuoteLineItem, which is how a single "Line Items" block produces the full table.

text
Section: Pricing Summary
+------------------+--------------------+--------------------+
| Line item name   | List price         | Net price          |
| (repeats per QLI)| (repeats per QLI)  | (repeats per QLI)  |
+------------------+--------------------+--------------------+
Section: Payment Terms
+--------------------------------------+---------------------+
| Payment schedule text (static)       | Total ARR token     |
+--------------------------------------+---------------------+

Standard vs custom templates

CPQ ships template categories, and a quote template is attached to a quote through either the quote record, the product family, or a per-quote override. The standard categories simplify maintenance: you centralize rules once and CPQ picks the right visual for each deal.

CategoryUse caseDelivery
StandardOne corporate layout for every productKeep in a shared folder
Per quoteRegional or deal-specific formattingSelected on the Quote record
Attached via product familyProduct-line branding (cloud vs on-prem)Inherited from the family
CustomFull control over HTML, logos, and layout geometryOrderable, section-by-section

Template variables are the substitution engine: a dropdown list of merge fields you can drop into any text block. When you place a variable in a template, CPQ substitutes the corresponding value from the Quote or QuoteLineItem at render time. Variables cover quote standard fields, custom fields, and child line data.

💡
Tip: Any field you want available for merging must be added to the template variable picklist. Custom fields do not appear automatically.

The template layout: header, body, and footer

A template is organized into three functional areas, even though they are just sections and blocks at a specific position.

  • Header — logo, quote number, expiration date, account name, rep. Usually the first section, spanning the full width.
  • Body — the meat: line item tables, discount summaries, payment terms, disclaimer text, and any repeating blocks bound to lines or bundles.
  • Footer — signature lines, legal disclaimers, page numbers; typically the last section.

The height of a section and the placement of blocks determine pagination. Blocks that are too tall push content to the next page, and a block set to "repeat with page" renders on every page — handy for a legal footer or a cont'd header.

The connection between template and quote is made by setting the template as the quote template on the Quote record. Legacy CPQ stores the rendered snapshot on the SBQQ__QuoteDocument__c object with fields such as the template used, the document body in base64, file type, and the record IDs of the Quote and its lines.

soql
SELECT Id, SBQQ__Quote__c, SBQQ__Template__c, SBQQ__DocumentBody__c,
       SBQQ__FileType__c, SBQQ__GeneratedOn__c
FROM SBQQ__QuoteDocument__c
WHERE SBQQ__Quote__r.Name = 'Q-00123'
ORDER BY SBQQ__GeneratedOn__c DESC

Tokens, formulas, and block substitution

Template variables cover most needs, but real templates get dynamic with formulas and conditions. A block can be configured to render only when a condition holds — for example, only render the "Discount applied" block when Quote.Discount_Percent__c > 0. That keeps clean quotes for list-price deals and transparent ones for discounted deals.

  • Token substitution: {{Quote.Total_ARR__c}} style merge during render.
  • Conditional visibility: render a block only when a rule passes.
  • Formula output: compute values from multiple fields at render time (e.g., per-unit blended discount across lines).
  • Repeating blocks: bind a block to quote lines so it iterates once per line.
text
If Quote.Discount_Percent__c > 0 then render:
  "Your negotiated discount of {{Quote.Discount_Percent__c}}% has been applied
   to this proposal and your net total is {{Quote.Total_Price}}."
Else render:
  "This proposal is quoted at full list price."

Because the render happens when the document is generated, the document is a point-in-time snapshot. Re-pricing the quote after generation does not change an already-generated document — you must regenerate it. This is deliberate: it protects the agreed commercial terms.

Multi-language quote layouts

For global rollouts, a single template can carry multiple language translations. You define the translations on the quote template and select the language that should render. Full translations cover every text token; partial fallback keeps the default language for untranslated tokens, which is a pragmatic pattern for rolling out French or Spanish without waiting for 100% coverage.

ConfigurationBehavior
Default template languageFallback for any missing translation
Language per templateSelect on the template record
Language per quoteOverride on the Quote record
Account-derived languageConvenient for accounts in a single locale

Managing translations is an exercise in keeping object text in sync with your translation workbench strings. A common hygiene rule: translate for the markets you invoice — the signed document should match the language your legal team can defend.

Generating, delivering, and e-signing documents

Once a template is in place, generating a document is a single button action on the quote: CPQ renders the document, stores a copy, and attaches it to the quote record. You control the generated file type (PDF is the default and safest for external sharing; Word preserves editability for redline).

Delivery options depend on org configuration and installed packages:

  • Attach to quote — the generated document becomes an attachment or Content document on the Quote.
  • Email — a template-driven email includes the generated PDF as an attachment.
  • eSignature — with an e-signature package, the quote document is sent for signature directly; the signed copy and status flow back and update the Quote. A signed quote is typically the gate that lets a quote progress to Contract or Order creation.
apex
// Examples of the data a doc-generation routine reads before rendering
List<Quote> quotes = [SELECT Id, Name, Total_ARR__c, Discount_Percent__c,
                             Approval_Status__c, Contract_Term_Months__c
                      FROM Quote WHERE CPQ_Sync_Status__c = 'Ready'];

Set<Id> quoteIds = new Set<Id>();
for (Quote q : quotes) {
    quoteIds.add(q.Id);
}

// Lines that will be repeated into the line-items block
List<QuoteLineItem> lines = [SELECT QuoteId, List_Unit_Price__c, Net_Unit_Price__c,
                                    ARR__c, Is_Bundle_Parent__c, Bundle_Option__c
                             FROM QuoteLineItem WHERE QuoteId IN :quoteIds];
💡
Tip: Regenerate the document after any pricing change that moved approval status. Shipping a stale PDF is one of the most common audit findings in real implementations.

Hands-on walkthrough: build a quote template and generate a document

This walkthrough uses the CPQ & Revenue Cloud Academy data model and the QuoteCalculatorService available in your lab org.

  1. Create a template folder named Academy_Standard using the CPQ template folders list.
  2. Create a quote template in that folder and name it Academy HWM Quote. Leave the default language set to en_US.

  3. Add a Header section spanning full width. Inside it add a block of type Text:

    • Logo placeholders and the token {{Quote.Name}}.
    • A conditional block that only renders when Quote.Is_Renewal__c is true: Renewal of {{Quote.Account.Name}}.
  4. Add a Pricing Summary section. Add one block of type Line Items bound to quote lines so it repeats per line, plus a block showing {{Quote.Total_Price}} and {{Quote.Total_ARR__c}}.
  5. Add a Terms section with the payment-terms text and a Signature block for the footer.
  6. Open a quote in the lab org, confirm Approval_Status__c is Approved, and attach the template to the quote.
  7. Run the Apex snippet below to refresh quote totals before render, then generate the document with the Generate Document action.
apex
// Before rendering, use the academy calculator service to freshen pricing
List<Id> ids = new List<Id>{ '00Q6g000000XyAb' }; // a real quote Id in your org
QuoteCalculatorService.recalculate(ids);
  1. Confirm the SBQQ__QuoteDocument__c record exists, has SBQQ__FileType__c = PDF, and its generated-on timestamp is later than the recalculation.
  2. Verify the document shows the multi-language template: switch the quote's language to fr_FR per account Region__c = 'EMEA' where translations exist, and regenerate.
  3. Attach the generated PDF to the quote and send it for e-signature; confirm the signature status updates the Quote.

Common pitfalls

  • Forgetting that documents are snapshots — regenerating is mandatory after re-pricing, or the signed copy disagrees with the CRM total.
  • Custom fields missing from the merge picklist — if a token is empty, the field was likely never added to the template variables.
  • Overly wide sections — blocks beyond page width wrap unpredictably; keep grid widths to realistic page proportions.
  • Ignoring conditions — unconditionally rendering the discount block on a zero-discount quote looks sloppy to customers.
  • No naming convention for templates — "Copy of Copy of Template" folders collapse under their own weight in enterprise orgs.
  • Multilingual gaps — partial translations silently fall back; audit which languages still show default text before full rollout.

Key takeaways

  • Quote documents are the contractual hand-off point in quote-to-cash and a control gate for approvals, contracts, and orders.
  • Templates compose as folders → templates → sections → blocks, rendering into a point-in-time QuoteDocument.
  • Tokens, conditions, and repeating blocks make one template serve many deal shapes and languages.
  • PDF is the safe default; e-signature turns the quote into the binding artifact that unlocks downstream processes.
  • Always regenerate after pricing or approval changes so the customer-facing artifact matches the data in the platform.
